lead: 5/3/1 is a strength training template created by powerlifter and coach Jim Wendler. It builds around four main lifts (squat, bench press, deadlift, overhead press) with work sets of 5, 3 and 1 reps set from a conservative training max.
For looks, the payoff is the muscle and strength gained from steady, heavy compound lifting plus assistance work. Its author presents slow progression as a core principle.

paras: Wendler's beginner page describes three full-body days with the main lifts plus First Set Last volume, and assistance work in push, pull and single-leg or core categories, with conditioning on other days. Weights are based on a training max that is raised only if every rep meets form standards.
Risks are those of heavy barbell training, such as strain from poor form. Wendler's page advises keeping form uncompromised and going lighter when in doubt.

angle.text: The program organises progressive heavy lifting and assistance work, the inputs people use to build muscle. Lifters track the cycle to keep progress steady.

lead: 5/3/1 is a strength program devised by Jim Wendler, in which a lifter works from a training max and progresses through weeks of work sets in 5, 3 and 1 rep ranges. It is widely discussed on T Nation, where Wendler is a well-known contributor and where members share logs and opinions.[1][2]

A beginner version on Wendler's site describes three weekly full-body sessions: squat and bench on Monday, deadlift and press on Wednesday, bench and squat on Friday, each with 5/3/1 sets plus 5x5 at First Set Last, then 50-100 reps each of push, pull and single-leg or core assistance work.[3]
Appearance-wise, people use it to gain muscle mass and strength, which shapes the physique in shoulders, back, chest and legs.
infobox: Squat, bench press, deadlift, overhead press

paras: Percentages are based on a training max, and work sets build toward roughly 80-85 percent of it. The training max goes up only when every rep meets form standards.[3]
Each day adds assistance in push, pull and single-leg or core categories, and Wendler's beginner page lists conditioning on non-lifting days at moderate intensity.[3]
Wendler states that the program should be run as written, that form should never be compromised, and that strength and size depend on mastering basics.[3]
T Nation threads mention Wendler and his gym, and some members refer to his seminars.[1][2][4]
